questions.stem: At 0900 the nurse scans a client's wristband before giving metoprolol, but the scanner cannot read the worn barcode. The client is alert and states their name and date of birth correctly. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Type the medical record number into the system by hand and give the dose
Print and put on a new wristband, then scan it before giving the dose
Scan the spare label in the client's chart, since it has the same barcode
Give the dose after checking two identifiers, then report the scanner fault

rationale.correct: Barcode workarounds cause errors; fix the problem and complete the check rather than bypassing it.

perOption.a: Manual entry is a workaround that skips the check the barcode provides.
perOption.b: Fixing the cause keeps the barcode check in place; a short delay is safe for this dose.
perOption.c: A label that is not on the client does not confirm the client's identity.
perOption.d: Two identifiers are needed, but bypassing the scan removes a safety layer that can easily be restored.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing order-writing errors with new nurses. Which notations are on the Joint Commission "Do Not Use" list? Select all that apply.

options.text: "U" for units
"IU" for international units
"QD" for daily
A trailing zero, as in 5.0 mg
"MS" for morphine sulfate
A leading zero, as in 0.5 mg
"mL" for milliliters

rationale.correct: Write "units" and "international units", write "daily", always use leading zeros and never trailing zeros, and write out drug names.

perOption.a: It can be misread as 0 or 4, causing large insulin errors.
perOption.b: It can be misread as IV or 10.
perOption.c: It can be confused with QID.
perOption.d: The decimal point can be missed, causing a tenfold overdose.
perOption.e: It can be confused with magnesium sulfate.
perOption.f: Leading zeros are required before a decimal point.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is programming a smart pump for a heparin infusion at 18 units/kg/hr for a client who weighs 92 kg. The pump's drug library shows a hard-limit alert that the dose is too high and will not start. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Program the heparin as a basic infusion outside the drug library
Recheck the order, the bag concentration and the values entered
Ask the pharmacy to raise the hard limit for this client
Ask a second nurse to program the pump on a different channel

rationale.correct: Smart pump alerts are a safety net. Investigate the alert by checking the order, concentration and entry, rather than bypassing it.

perOption.a: Bypassing the library removes the safety check that just caught a possible error.
perOption.b: A hard-limit alert usually means a programming or calculation error, such as the wrong weight units or concentration.
perOption.c: Hard limits mark doses that are dangerous; the cause of the alert must be found first.
perOption.d: Another person or channel does not address why the alert fired.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing four medications for clients on a medical unit. Facility policy requires an independent double check by a second nurse for certain high-alert drugs. Which medication needs this check?

options.text: An IV regular insulin infusion
IV ondansetron 4 mg for nausea
Oral metoprolol tartrate 25 mg
IV pantoprazole 40 mg daily

rationale.correct: High-alert drugs such as insulin, heparin, IV opioids, concentrated potassium and chemotherapy often need independent double checks.

perOption.a: IV insulin is a high-alert medication; many facilities require an independent double check.
perOption.b: Ondansetron is not classed as a high-alert medication.
perOption.c: Oral beta-blockers are not classed as high-alert medications.
perOption.d: Pantoprazole is not a high-alert medication.

questions.stem: After a near miss, the pharmacy finds that hydroxyzine and hydralazine tablets are stored in neighboring bins in the unit's automated cabinet. Which change best reduces the risk of a mix-up?

options.text: Store the two drugs apart and label them with tall-man lettering
Remind nurses at each huddle to read the labels more carefully
Put a bright "Use caution" sticker on each of the two bins
Have the pharmacist approve every dose of either drug first

rationale.correct: System fixes such as separation, tall-man lettering and barcoding work better than reminders and warnings.

perOption.a: Separation plus tall-man lettering (hydrOXYzine, hydrALAZINE) is a system fix that reduces confusion.
perOption.b: Relying on vigilance alone is not a system fix.
perOption.c: A general warning is a weak strategy that staff quickly stop noticing.
perOption.d: This adds delay without addressing the storage problem.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing new medication orders on a medical unit before giving the 0900 doses. For each order, choose whether the nurse should give the medication or stop and clarify the order first.

rows.text: "Metoprolol 25 mg PO BID"; the heart rate is 78/min and blood pressure 134/82
"Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed" with no reason given
"Furosemide 40 mg IV daily"; the potassium is 4.2 mEq/L

rationale.correct: Clarify incomplete or error-prone orders before giving the medication; give complete orders when the client's data are safe.

perOption.r1:c1: The order is complete and the client's values are safe.
perOption.r1:c2: There is no reason to stop.
perOption.r2:c1: "U" could be read as 0, so 10 U might become 100.
perOption.r2:c2: Clarify and have the order rewritten with "units".
perOption.r3:c2: Clarify the indication, such as pain rated 4 to 6.
perOption.r4:c1: The order and the potassium level are acceptable.
perOption.r4:c2: There is no reason to stop.

questions.stem: An infant security alarm sounds on the postpartum unit, and the overhead page announces the facility's infant abduction code. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check that every infant is accounted for and watch the unit exits
Silence the alarm at the panel, then look for the cause of the alert
Go to the parking garage to look for anyone carrying an infant
Wait at the nurses' station until security arrives and gives orders

rationale.correct: Infant abduction prevention relies on ID bands, security tags, staff identification and a practiced code response.

perOption.a: The abduction code calls for securing exits and accounting for every infant right away.
perOption.b: The alarm must be treated as real until every infant is accounted for.
perOption.c: Staff follow the code on the unit; security handles the wider search.
perOption.d: Staff act immediately according to the code.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching new parents on the postpartum unit how to keep their newborn safe from abduction. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hand your baby only to staff wearing the unit's special photo ID badge
Keep the bassinet on the side of the bed away from the door
Do not post the baby's photo or room number on social media
Leave the baby in the room while you shower if the door is closed
Let a visitor you know take the baby for a walk in the hallway

rationale.correct: Teach parents to check staff identity, keep the infant within sight and limit public details.

perOption.a: Abductors may pose as staff.
perOption.b: This makes quick removal harder.
perOption.c: Public details help abductors.
perOption.d: The baby is never left alone.
perOption.e: Infants stay in the room with the parents.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: An overhead page announces an active shooter on the floor below. The nurse is in a hallway near the stairwell with two clients who can walk. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Take the clients down the stairwell if it is safe; hide if not
Move the clients into the hallway so that they can all be counted
Pull the nearest fire alarm so that the whole building leaves at once
Go to the nurses' station so that the police can find the staff

rationale.correct: Active shooter response is run, hide, fight; secure clients in locked rooms when evacuation is not possible.

perOption.a: "Run, hide, fight": leave if there is a safe route, hide and lock in if not, and fight only as a last resort.
perOption.b: Gathering people in a hallway exposes them to danger.
perOption.c: A fire alarm can draw people into the shooter's path.
perOption.d: The station is exposed; staff protect themselves and clients first.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A visitor upset about a long wait raises their voice, clenches their fists and steps toward the nurse at the nurses' station. Which action by the nurse is safest?

options.text: Step between the visitor and the exit so the visitor cannot leave
Keep a safe distance, speak calmly, keep an exit open and call security
Turn away and return to charting to show the visitor you are not afraid
Raise your voice firmly so the visitor knows you are in control

rationale.correct: Workplace violence: keep distance, keep an exit, de-escalate and get help early.

perOption.a: Blocking an exit can escalate the situation.
perOption.b: Distance, a calm tone, an escape route and early help protect staff.
perOption.c: Never turn your back on someone who is threatening.
perOption.d: Raising your voice escalates the situation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with dementia was found at the main entrance trying to leave the hospital and has been brought back safely. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Apply a vest restraint whenever the client is in bed at night
Ask the provider for a PRN sedative to keep the client in bed
Assess elopement risk, use a wander-alert band and increase supervision
Move the client to the room nearest the stairwell for easier watching

rationale.correct: Elopement prevention uses risk assessment, wander-alert devices, supervision and engagement, not restraint.

perOption.a: Restraints are not the first response and raise the risk of injury.
perOption.b: A chemical restraint is a last resort.
perOption.c: Least restrictive measures, such as alert devices, supervision and engagement, reduce elopement risk.
perOption.d: A room near an exit makes elopement easier; a room near the nurses' station is better.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The perioperative nurse is preparing a client with diabetes for an elective colectomy. Which actions are part of a surgical site infection (SSI) prevention bundle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Giving the prophylactic antibiotic within 60 minutes before the incision
Removing hair with clippers rather than a razor, if hair removal is needed
Keeping blood glucose controlled before, during and after surgery
Keeping the client warm during surgery
Shaving the operative site the night before surgery
Continuing prophylactic antibiotics for 7 days after surgery

rationale.correct: SSI prevention: timely antibiotics, clippers instead of razors, glucose control and normothermia.

perOption.a: This gives effective tissue levels at the time of incision.
perOption.b: Razors cause small cuts that raise infection risk.
perOption.c: Hyperglycemia increases SSI risk.
perOption.d: Normothermia supports immune function and healing.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An infection prevention nurse is teaching ICU staff about prevention bundles. For each intervention, choose the healthcare-associated infection or infections it helps prevent. Each row may have more than one answer.

rows.text: Hand hygiene before touching the device
Daily review of whether the device is still needed
Head of bed raised 30 to 45 degrees
Scrubbing the hub before each access
Keeping the drainage bag below the bladder

rationale.correct: Bundles share hand hygiene and daily device review; each also has device-specific steps.

perOption.r1:c3: Hand hygiene prevents transfer of organisms to the airway.
perOption.r2:c1: Remove catheters as soon as possible.
perOption.r2:c2: Remove central lines as soon as possible.
perOption.r2:c3: Daily sedation breaks and weaning checks shorten ventilation.
perOption.r3:c1: This is not related to urinary catheters.
perOption.r3:c2: This is not related to central lines.
perOption.r4:c1: This is not related to urinary catheters.
perOption.r4:c2: It removes bacteria from the access port.
perOption.r4:c3: This is not related to ventilation.
perOption.r5:c1: It prevents backflow into the bladder.
perOption.r5:c2: This is not related to central lines.
perOption.r5:c3: This is not related to ventilation.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse is moving a shared blood pressure cuff from one client's room to another on a medical unit. How should the nurse clean it?

options.text: Wipe it with an approved disinfectant for the label's contact time
Rinse it under warm running tap water and let it air-dry fully
Leave it uncleaned when there is no visible soil anywhere on the cuff
Send it to central sterile supply to be autoclaved before reuse

rationale.correct: Non-critical equipment needs disinfection, with the correct contact time, between clients.

perOption.a: Low-level disinfection with the right contact time kills common organisms.
perOption.b: Water does not disinfect.
perOption.c: Organisms can be present without visible soil.
perOption.d: Non-critical items need disinfection, not sterilization.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse on an oncology unit wakes up with a temperature of 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), a sore throat and a productive cough before a scheduled shift. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Work the shift while wearing a surgical mask at all times
Follow the employee health policy and stay away from clients
Ask to care only for clients who are not on chemotherapy
Take an antipyretic before the shift so the fever does not show

rationale.correct: Staff illness policies protect clients; staff with fever and respiratory symptoms stay home and follow employee health guidance.

perOption.a: A mask lowers but does not remove the risk to immunocompromised clients.
perOption.b: Staff with infectious illnesses stay away from clients, especially vulnerable ones.
perOption.c: Every client on the unit is still at risk.
perOption.d: This hides symptoms without reducing spread.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A new nurse is reviewing the hospital's vaccination requirements for staff. Which vaccine is recommended every year for health care workers?

options.text: Influenza
Hepatitis B
MMR
Tetanus

rationale.correct: Health care workers need annual influenza vaccine and proof of immunity to hepatitis B, MMR and varicella.

perOption.a: Annual influenza vaccination protects staff and clients.
perOption.b: Hepatitis B is a series with proof of immunity, not yearly.
perOption.c: MMR is usually 2 lifetime doses or proof of immunity.
perOption.d: Tetanus is boosted every 10 years.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in the clinic waiting room is coughing and sneezing repeatedly. Other clients, including a mother with a newborn, are seated nearby. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Offer the client a mask and tissues and a seat away from others
Ask the client to wait outside until the provider is ready
Move the mother and newborn to an exam room and leave the client
Ask the provider to prescribe an antibiotic before the visit

rationale.correct: Respiratory hygiene: masks, tissues, hand hygiene and distance for anyone with respiratory symptoms.

perOption.a: Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette reduce spread right away.
perOption.b: The client still needs care, and sending them outside is not necessary.
perOption.c: Moving one family helps them but does not stop the spread to others.
perOption.d: Antibiotics are not indicated and do not stop the spread now.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who returned 10 days ago from an area with an Ebola outbreak arrives with a fever, vomiting and diarrhea. The client is placed in a private room. Which precautions should the nurse use?

options.text: Full PPE put on and taken off with a trained observer watching
Airborne isolation with a fit-tested N95 respirator and no gown
Contact precautions with a standard isolation gown and gloves
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask and protective goggles

rationale.correct: High-consequence infections such as Ebola need strict PPE protocols with a trained observer during donning and doffing.

perOption.a: Ebola spreads through body fluids; a trained observer prevents self-contamination during donning and doffing.
perOption.b: Ebola is spread by body fluids, and an N95 alone does not protect the skin and mucous membranes.
perOption.c: Standard contact precautions do not give enough protection for Ebola.
perOption.d: Droplet precautions do not protect against heavy body-fluid exposure.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is completing the screening checklist for a client scheduled for an MRI of the lumbar spine. Which finding should the nurse report to the radiology team before the scan?

options.text: The client is allergic to shellfish and iodine
The client had a pacemaker placed 8 years ago
The client had a titanium hip replacement 2 years ago
The client takes metformin for type 2 diabetes

rationale.correct: MRI screening asks about implanted devices, pacemakers, metal fragments and patches containing metal; contrast-related questions differ between CT and MRI.

perOption.a: Iodine allergy matters for CT contrast; MRI uses gadolinium and the magnet is the main concern.
perOption.b: Many older pacemakers are not MRI-safe; the magnet can affect device function or heat the leads.
perOption.c: Most modern joint implants are MRI-safe, though the team notes them.
perOption.d: Metformin is held for iodinated CT contrast, not for MRI.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department is in ventricular fibrillation, and the nurse is about to deliver a shock with a manual defibrillator. The client is on oxygen by nonrebreather mask and has a nitroglycerin patch on the chest. What should the nurse do immediately before delivering the shock?

options.text: Make sure no one is touching the client or bed, and call "all clear"
Leave the oxygen mask flowing so that the client stays well oxygenated
Place the pads over the nitroglycerin patch to save time
Wipe the chest with a wet cloth to improve contact with the pads

rationale.correct: Before defibrillation: clear everyone, move oxygen away, remove medication patches and make sure the chest is dry.

perOption.a: Clearing everyone prevents staff from being shocked.
perOption.b: Oxygen flowing near the pads is a fire risk; it is moved away during the shock.
perOption.c: Patches are removed and the skin wiped, because they can cause burns.
perOption.d: A wet chest can conduct current across the skin and cause burns.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a client with COPD to radiology on a stretcher with a portable oxygen cylinder. Which action is correct?

options.text: Lay the cylinder flat on the stretcher next to the client's legs
Secure the cylinder upright in a holder on the stretcher
Carry the cylinder by its valve while pushing the stretcher
Rest the cylinder against the radiology waiting-room heater

rationale.correct: Secure oxygen cylinders upright in a holder and keep them away from heat.

perOption.a: An unsecured cylinder can roll, fall and damage the valve.
perOption.b: A holder keeps the cylinder from falling and protects the valve.
perOption.c: A damaged valve can turn the cylinder into a projectile.
perOption.d: Heat raises the pressure in the cylinder and the risk of fire.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse is splashed in both eyes with a disinfectant while cleaning a spill. The eyes are burning and watering. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Flush both eyes at the eyewash station for at least 15 minutes
Read the product's safety data sheet to find the right first aid
Go straight to employee health to have the eyes examined
Cover both eyes with gauze pads and report the injury

rationale.correct: Chemical eye exposure: flush immediately for at least 15 minutes, then check the SDS and report.

perOption.a: Immediate, prolonged flushing limits the injury.
perOption.b: Flushing comes first; the SDS is checked afterward.
perOption.c: Delaying flushing increases the damage.
perOption.d: Covering the eyes traps the chemical against them.

The unit's infection-control binder
The facility's drug reference guide
The label on the cleaning cart

perOption.a: The SDS lists hazards, handling, PPE and first aid.
perOption.b: This covers procedures, not chemical hazards.
perOption.c: Drug references do not cover cleaning chemicals.
perOption.d: The cart label is not a full hazard reference.

questions.stem: While giving an injection, the nurse notices that the sharps container in the client's room is about three-quarters full and a needle cap is sticking out of the opening. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Push the contents down gently to make room for more sharps
Close and replace the container according to the unit's policy
Keep using it until the fill line printed on the container is reached
Tape over the opening and put it in the regular trash

rationale.correct: Replace sharps containers when about three-quarters full, and never push the contents down.

perOption.a: Pushing sharps down can cause needlestick injuries.
perOption.b: Containers are closed and replaced when about three-quarters full.
perOption.c: A container this full is a needlestick risk and is replaced now.
perOption.d: Sharps containers are regulated medical waste.

questions.stem: The circulating nurse is reviewing fire risks before a procedure on the upper chest. Which situation creates the greatest risk of a surgical fire?

options.text: Using the electrosurgical pencil near open oxygen while the alcohol prep is still wet
Using a forced-air warming blanket set to a medium temperature during surgery
Counting sponges and instruments before the incision and again before closing
Using a water-based skin prep that has fully dried before the drapes are placed

rationale.correct: Surgical fires need an ignition source, fuel and oxygen. Let alcohol preps dry fully and keep oxygen away from the surgical site.

perOption.a: An ignition source, fuel (alcohol) and oxygen together make up the fire triangle.
perOption.b: Warming blankets are not an ignition source in normal use.
perOption.c: Counts prevent retained items; they do not cause fire.
perOption.d: A dry, nonflammable prep lowers the fire risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At the end of an abdominal surgery, the final sponge count is one fewer than the opening count. The surgeon says, "The count was probably wrong at the start; let's close." What should happen?

options.text: Close the incision and recount the sponges once in the recovery room
Recount, search the field and get an x-ray before the client leaves
Document the discrepancy on the record and let the surgeon close
Agree that the first count was wrong and correct the count sheet

rationale.correct: Count discrepancies are resolved before closure, with an x-ray if needed; the nurse speaks up even when the surgeon disagrees.

perOption.a: A retained item must be ruled out before the incision is closed.
perOption.b: The discrepancy is resolved before closure, with imaging if the sponge is not found.
perOption.c: Documenting alone does not prevent a retained item.
perOption.d: A count discrepancy is never assumed to be a counting mistake.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A fire on a nearby unit means the charge nurse has ordered a horizontal evacuation of the medical unit to the next smoke compartment. Place the clients in the order they should be moved, from first to last.

items.text: A final sweep of rooms to confirm no one is left behind
Clients who can walk with guidance

rationale.correct: Horizontal evacuation usually moves the most independent clients first so the most lives are saved quickly, then confirms the unit is empty.

perOption.a: Moving the most mobile clients first gets the most people to safety quickly.
perOption.b: These clients move next, as they need some help.
perOption.c: They are moved last because they need the most staff and equipment.
perOption.d: The unit is checked and marked empty.

questions.stem: A nurse at the nurses' station answers a phone call. A calm voice says there is a bomb in the hospital and it will go off in an hour. What should the nurse do?

Keep the caller talking, note the details, then notify security
Begin evacuating the unit right away without telling anyone else
Search clients' rooms and belongings for anything suspicious

perOption.a: Keeping the caller talking gathers information that helps the response.
perOption.b: Details about the caller, timing and location help security respond.
perOption.c: The facility's plan decides whether and how to evacuate.
perOption.d: Staff do not search or touch suspicious items.

options.text: Have backup oxygen cylinders and a plan if the power goes out
Turn the oxygen off during the storm to reduce the fire risk
Keep the spare cylinders next to the generator so they stay handy
Make a plan with the family once the storm has reached the area

rationale.correct: Clients who depend on powered medical equipment need backup power and supplies before a disaster.

perOption.a: Concentrators need electricity, so a backup supply and power plan are essential.
perOption.b: Stopping oxygen is unsafe for a client who needs it continuously.
perOption.c: Oxygen near a generator is a fire risk.
perOption.d: Planning must happen before the storm.

questions.stem: The nurse is observing a new graduate give morning medications on a busy medical unit. Highlight the actions that are unsafe.

segments.text: identified the client using name and date of birth
prepared medications for two clients at the same time
crushed an extended-release tablet to mix with applesauce
signed the medication record before giving the medication

rationale.correct: Prepare one client's medications at a time, do not crush extended-release forms, and document after giving.

perOption.s4: Preparing medications for more than one client at once increases mix-ups.
perOption.s6: Crushing extended-release forms releases the full dose at once.
perOption.s10: Documenting before giving can record medications that were never given.

questions.stem: While the nurse is giving morning medications, a client who takes levothyroxine at home says, "That pill is a different color from the one I usually take." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that hospital pharmacies often stock a different brand
Hold the pill and check it against the order and with the pharmacy
Give the pill now, and look into the color difference after the round
Ask the client to take it now, since it is a routine thyroid pill

rationale.correct: Always stop and verify when a client questions a medication.

perOption.a: This may be true, but it dismisses a possible error without checking.
perOption.b: A client's concern is an important safety check; verify before giving.
perOption.c: Giving first could cause harm if it is the wrong drug.
perOption.d: Every medication is verified when the client questions it.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with poorly controlled epilepsy who had two seizures at home this week is admitted to a medical unit. Select the 3 actions that best reduce the client's risk of injury.

options.text: Pad the side rails of the bed
Keep suction and oxygen ready at the bedside
Keep the bed in its lowest position
Keep a padded tongue blade at the bedside
Raise all four side rails as a restraint
Take oral temperatures with a glass thermometer

rationale.correct: Seizure precautions protect the client from injury and support the airway; they do not include restraint or objects in the mouth.

perOption.a: Padding prevents injury if a seizure happens in bed.
perOption.b: These support the airway after a seizure.
perOption.c: A low bed reduces injury from a fall.
perOption.d: Nothing is put in the mouth during a seizure.
perOption.e: Raised rails can count as a restraint and do not prevent seizures.
perOption.f: Glass can break if the client has a seizure.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
